paragraphs.heading: What orogeny is
paragraphs.text: Orogeny is the process that builds mountains. It takes place at a convergent plate margin, when the motion of the plates squeezes that margin. The squeezed plate crumples and is lifted up into one or more mountain ranges. The belt that develops this way is called an orogenic belt, or orogen. The word comes from Ancient Greek óros, 'mountain', and génesis, 'creation' or 'origin'.

paragraphs.heading: More than crumpling
paragraphs.text: Mountain building involves a series of geological processes, together called orogenesis. Some of them deform continental crust that already exists. Others create new continental crust through volcanism. Magma rising inside the orogen carries less dense material upward and leaves denser material behind. The result is that Earth's lithosphere, meaning its crust and uppermost mantle, becomes differentiated in composition.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to converge
paragraphs.text: Orogeny happens on the convergent margins of continents, and the convergence may take two forms. One is subduction, in which a continent rides forcefully over an oceanic plate. The result is a noncollisional orogen. The Andes Mountains are one such belt, and belts of this kind are sometimes named Andean-type orogens. The other form is continental collision, where two or more continents converge and form a collisional orogen.

paragraphs.heading: When subduction builds mountains
paragraphs.text: Subduction zones use up oceanic crust, thicken the lithosphere, and produce earthquakes and volcanoes. Yet not every subduction zone produces an orogenic belt. Mountains are built only when the subduction compresses the overriding plate. Whether that happens depends on factors such as how fast the plates converge and how strongly the two plates are coupled. The coupling may in turn depend on factors such as the angle of subduction and how fast sediment builds up in the oceanic trench that goes with the subduction zone.

paragraphs.heading: How continents grow
paragraphs.text: As subduction goes on, island arcs, pieces of continent and oceanic material may gradually attach to the continental margin. This is one of the main ways continents have grown. An orogen built from such crustal fragments, called terranes, added over a long time with no sign of a major collision between continents, is an accretionary orogen. The North American Cordillera is an example. The orogeny may culminate when continental crust from the far side of the subducting oceanic plate arrives at the subduction zone. That ends subduction and turns the orogen into a collisional one of the Himalayan type, which may raise extremely high mountains, as has been happening in the Himalayas over the last 65 million years.

paragraphs.heading: Slow and long-lived
paragraphs.text: Orogeny can go on for tens of millions of years, building mountains from what used to be sedimentary basins. Activity along one orogenic belt can last an extremely long time. On the west coast of North America, a sequence of orogenies opened with the Antler orogeny in the late Devonian, roughly 380 million years ago. It went on with the Sonoma and Sevier orogenies and culminated with the Laramide orogeny. The Laramide orogeny by itself ran for 40 million years, starting 75 million years ago and ending 35 million years ago.

paragraphs.heading: Young belts and old belts
paragraphs.text: Orogenic belts are long regions of deformation that border cratons, the stable interiors of continents. Young belts, where subduction is still going on, have frequent volcanic activity and earthquakes. Older belts are typically worn down deeply by erosion, which exposes displaced and deformed strata. These are often strongly metamorphosed, and they include vast bodies of intrusive igneous rock known as batholiths.
